narrative.text: A cover page, partly garbled by OCR, bearing the document code WHO/PUB/TPS/93.1, the World Health Organization, Geneva, and the year 1993.

The first contents page of the editorial style manual, listing sections 1 to 8 (introduction, spelling, punctuation, italics, footnotes, quotations, transliteration, and copyright and disclaimers) with their subsections and page numbers.

The second contents page, listing sections 9 to 14 on reference lists, manuscript mark-up, abbreviations and symbols, numbers and units, mathematics and statistics, and scientific terminology, with subsections and page numbers.

The third contents page, listing sections 15 to 18 on non-discriminatory language, sensitive topics, technical reports and reference books, plus four annexes on spelling, Member States, place names and mark-up terms, with page numbers.
A near-empty page with no text.

Introduces the manual as a reference for WHO editors working in English, meant to keep language clear and terminology and symbols consistent, to be consulted in cases of doubt rather than applied rigidly. States that it is not a grammar or writing guide, names the unit that prepared it and invites comments.
A near-empty page with no text.

Introduces the spelling section, stating that British spelling is normally used, following the first spelling in the Concise Oxford Dictionary, with exceptions such as established WHO usage, international nomenclature, quotations and titles. Begins the discussion of medical and scientific terminology, listing exceptions such as fetal and estrogen and pointing to the International Nomenclature of Diseases.

Continues the spelling section, advising against eponymous disease names and the possessive form, and recommending medical dictionaries. Covers country and place names, directing editors to a terminology subunit and annexes, and begins the syllabification topic.

Gives rules for hyphenation: hyphens after prefixes to prevent misreading or double letters, and with compound nouns and adjectives depending on use. Advises introducing hyphens only to avoid ambiguity.
Begins a list of hyphenated terms common in WHO publications, from above-mentioned to roughly the letter L, such as case-study, cut-off point and follow-up.
Continues the list of hyphenated terms common in WHO publications, from last-mentioned to X-ray, such as long-term, policy-maker, side-effects and well-being.

Explains capitalization, saying proper names, titles and institutions take capitals while descriptive appellations do not, and covers trade names and Linnaean genus names. Lists words normally capitalized in WHO usage, such as Member State, the Organization, Secretariat and Region, with others capitalized only when specific.

Lists words and expressions not normally capitalized, such as committee, health for all, primary health care and resolution, and refers to an Oxford reference for more. Also explains the preference for -ize over -ise, with exceptions where -ise is part of the root and where -yse is required.
Gives rules for alphabetical arrangement in lists and indexes, covering name particles such as de or von, Mac and Mc prefixes, Chinese family names and chemical names.

Begins the punctuation section, advising that punctuation should be minimal and clarify meaning, and gives rules on the full point, including where it is omitted and how it combines with other marks. Points readers to further reading.

Gives guidance on the comma, including consistency before the final and in lists and use to avoid ambiguity, and the semicolon, which links closely related clauses. Begins the discussion of the colon.
Continues the punctuation section with the three uses of the colon, then parentheses, and dashes, covering hyphens and the en rule with examples.
Continues with en rule uses, including ranges, then the em rule and its uses, and the use of square brackets for interpolations in quotations.
Covers question marks, necessary for direct but not indirect questions, and lists books recommended for further reading on punctuation and editing.
A near-empty page with no text.
Explains when italics are used in WHO publications, including titles, uncommon foreign words, variables and scientific terms, and lists foreign expressions to italicize or print in roman.
Gives brief italics guidance: variables and scientific terms refer to other sections, and italics for emphasis should be used sparingly.

Explains when and how to use footnotes, which should be kept to a minimum, with long material put in annexes, and how to identify them with numerals, letters or special signs. Notes numbering and repeating marks for the same footnote. The text is cut off at the end.
Completes the footnotes guidance: placement after quotation marks, distinguishing editor's notes from the author's, and paragraphing, with each footnote ending with a full stop.

Sets rules for quotations, covering exact fidelity to the original, three spaced dots for omissions, square brackets for inserted words, and when to set long quotations apart. It also explains quotation-mark nesting and placement of punctuation relative to quotation marks.
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Begins the section on transliteration, saying Arabic, Russian and Chinese are romanized and that doubtful cases go to the language services office. It gives rules for Arabic names (such as the hyphenated lower-case article al and the inseparable Abd) and recommends an ISO system for Russian.

Continues the transliteration section, advising that a person's preferred spelling of their name be respected, and requiring the pinyin system for Chinese in all WHO publications, with notes on accents, apostrophes and given names.

Explains that accepted manuscripts become the Organization's property and reproduces the standard copyright notice and disclaimers printed on the verso of the title page. The disclaimers cover permission to reproduce or translate, country and boundary designations, and the mention of companies or products.

Gives a disclaimer wording for meeting reports and sets out the rules for reproducing previously published material. It says the originating unit must obtain permission, treats short quotations with a source as fair use, and requires permission for drawings, tables and photographs.

Opens the section on reference lists and bibliographies, distinguishing a list of cited works from a bibliography of recommended reading and setting rules for each. It also says the numerical citation system is preferred (and obligatory for some series) and how to cite unpublished findings.

Shows how numerical and Harvard citations appear in the text, then begins the bibliographic style based on the Vancouver style with WHO adaptations. It lists the basic rules (author listing, full journal names, punctuation) and gives example entries for articles, books and book chapters.

Gives further example reference formats, including monographs in a series, corporate authors, WHO publications without a named author, dissertations, conference proceedings papers and unpublished documents available to readers.

Explains how reference lists are ordered and adapted for the Harvard system, including ordering rules for single and multiple authors and same-year works distinguished by letters. It also begins guidance on typographical style, such as italics for titles of books and journals.

Begins the section on manuscript mark-up and layout, listing the limited mark-up editors need to supply (headings, symbols, type requirements, figure and table positions, spacing). It also says printer instructions should be circled and what preliminary pages go to the typesetter.
Gives rules for presenting tables: keep them simple, avoid vertical rules, make units in headings unambiguous, avoid blank cells, and use lettered or symbol footnote marks.
Finishes the guidance on table elements (source line, notes, acknowledgements) and on checking tables for internal consistency and agreement with the text. It includes an annotated example table.

Begins the rules for list formats, describing Formats 1 and 2 for numbered lists and sub-items with their capitalisation, punctuation and indentation conventions, and starting Format 3 for bulleted lists.
Continues the list formats, covering bulleted items (Formats 3 and 4), dash lists of short items with and without end punctuation (Formats 5 and 6), and bullets used for emphasis (Format 7).
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Begins the section on abbreviations and symbols, explaining their purpose, the need to define them at first use, and caution against overuse or confusing forms. It describes the ways abbreviations and symbols are structured, such as truncating the end or suppressing the middle of a word.
Gives a further-reading list on units, symbols and abbreviations and a table of common abbreviations (such as cf., e.g., etc., et al., Fig., Vol.) with notes on where particular forms are used.
Starts a list of abbreviations of international and other organizations most often met in WHO documents, giving each acronym with its full name.
Continues the list of organization acronyms with their full names; extraction has separated the acronym column from the names column, so the two appear as separate runs.

Lists commonly used symbols for units of measurement, including the SI base units, and says they are used only after figures, in tables and in graphs. It also gives the SI prefixes for forming multiples and submultiples.
Points to reference works with extensive lists of medical abbreviations and begins an alphabetical list of common medical-science acronyms, marking those that need not be defined.
Continues the alphabetical list of medical-science abbreviations and acronyms with their expansions, from FSH onward; extraction has separated the abbreviations from their expansions.

Gives guidance on units of currency, citing sources for official currency names and abbreviations. It says to distinguish same-named currencies and gives rules for placing amounts, abbreviations and symbols.
Covers abbreviation of compass points in latitude, longitude, tables and figures, and lists two-letter abbreviations for United States states and territories.
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Opens the section on numbers, dates, time and units of measurement, giving rules for when to use words or figures, thin-space grouping of digits, decimal points, exponential notation, the ambiguous word billion and the spacing of ratios.

Continues the rules on units, requiring figures with unit symbols, limiting use of the solidus, and permitting certain exceptions for blood pressure and energy values. It also gives guidance on concentration and begins relative molecular mass.
Opens the section on mathematics and statistics, with rules for setting equations: italic variables, roman operators, bracket order, spacing, compact formulae and breaking long displayed equations.

Lists standard statistical terms with their symbols (such as mean, variance, standard deviation, degrees of freedom and significance level) and common abbreviations like CI and SD. It advises supporting means with measures of variability and warns against presenting variability in a misleading form.

Opens the section on scientific terminology, giving rules for anatomical terms and for naming animals, plants, bacteria and viruses, including italicizing genus and species names and the use of common names.

Continues scientific terminology with a note that bacterial and viral nomenclature codes differ, a further-reading list of nomenclature codes, and the beginning of guidance on biochemistry nomenclature.
Lists the three-letter and one-letter symbols for the common amino acids, then gives short guidance on enzyme nomenclature with a further-reading list.
Gives symbols for nucleosides and sugars used in sequences, figures and tables, then begins the chemistry guidance on IUPAC naming and preferred spellings such as sulfur, aluminium and caesium.

Continues chemistry conventions, covering how carbon-chain and carbon-atom designations and oxidation numbers are written. It also gives a further-reading list and begins rules for isotopic labelling.

Finishes the rules on italicized chemical prefixes and capitalization, then says disease names should follow the International Nomenclature of Diseases or standard dictionaries. It notes that ICD-10 is a statistical classification, not a nomenclature reference.
Gives a further-reading list on drug and pesticide names, then begins the genetics guidance on naming genes and chromosomes.
Continues gene nomenclature with prefixes for viral, nuclear and cellular genes, and sets out the naming convention for restriction enzymes with examples and a reference.
Gives conventions for naming haemoglobins and their chains and for noting amino acid substitutions in abnormal haemoglobins, with a further-reading list.
Gives the notation for interferons and interleukins, with examples and references, and begins a miscellaneous section pointing to other published nomenclature recommendations.
Lists published nomenclature references for complement components and the HLA system, then begins a short note on vitamin names.
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Opens the section on non-discriminatory language, explaining that its guidelines focus mainly on avoiding sex discrimination but apply to other bias too. It argues that language shapes equality and that sexist wording can diminish or offend women.
Argues that rewriting to remove discriminatory language need not be more cumbersome, with before-and-after examples about patients and pronouns, and begins practical rewriting suggestions.
Presents a table of common discriminatory phrases with suggested alternatives and general rules, such as deleting redundant pronouns, using the first person plural and replacing words built on man.

Continues the table of discriminatory phrases and alternatives, covering neutral job titles, avoiding assumptions about household roles, using a person's preferred name, varying the order of paired terms and avoiding gendered stereotyping adjectives.

Notes occasional exceptions where a man-based term is unavoidable and stresses editorial judgement. It also gives guidance on avoiding racial, cultural and age-related bias, including a substitution test and preferred terms for older people.
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Opens the section on politically and legally sensitive topics, warning editors to watch for terminology and statements that could offend Member States or involve disputed names. It says text criticizing or describing a government should be cleared by the government concerned through the technical unit.

Continues the guidance on sensitive topics, covering how to label territories and non-self-governing areas, the requirement that maps follow United Nations practice, and the start of examples of specific designations, beginning with Taiwan.

Covers care in using the term United Kingdom for legal and health-service matters and advises naming the constituent country in non-political contexts. It also says generic names should be preferred to trade names so that WHO does not appear to endorse products, with the start of rules for proprietary names.
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Opens the section on Technical Report Series manuscripts, explaining that these are reports of expert groups whose members approved the text, so editing must be cautious and major restructuring or large additions and deletions are not possible. It describes the purpose of expert group reports and begins the guidance on their structure.

Gives rules for the list of participants in an expert group report, covering heading, alphabetical order, titles and institutions, identification of officers, representatives of other organizations and the Secretariat.

Continues the technical reports guidance, warning against overt criticism of governments or WHO units, overgeneralizations and legally contentious statements. It also gives rules on how expert-group specifications and definitions may be described relative to WHO's own.

Gives rules for references in technical reports (consecutive numbering, placement before annexes, limited citing of unpublished WHO documents) and begins guidance on bibliographies as background reading.
Lists useful reference books, beginning with dictionaries and style manuals, as bibliographic entries.
Continues the list of reference books, covering works on English usage, style and editing such as writing guides, copy-editing handbooks and punctuation guides.
Lists reference books on scientific, technical and medical terminology and usage, including works on units and symbols, chemical and enzyme nomenclature and disability reporting guidelines.

Continues the list of reference books on scientific and medical terminology, including nonproprietary drug names, disease classification, units, chemical nomenclature, acronym dictionaries and pesticide indexes.
Finishes the reference-book list with further statistics, terminology and abbreviation works and begins a miscellaneous group that includes currency and country references.
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Opens Annex 1 on spelling, stating the general rule to follow the latest Concise Oxford Dictionary (first-listed variant) and that WHO has exceptions. It begins the alphabetical word list with preferred spellings and usage notes, starting at A.
Continues the alphabetical spelling list, from words beginning with an- through A and B, giving preferred WHO spellings and usage notes such as artefact, apnoea and bibliographic.

Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list through the letter C and into the start of the next section, giving preferred forms and distinctions between similar words such as complement and compliment.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list for words beginning with D, giving preferred spellings, distinctions between similar words and capitalization, hyphenation and compounding choices.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list for words beginning with F, giving preferred spellings and rules for hyphenation, compounding and capitalization.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list for words beginning with G and H, with preferred spellings such as haemoglobin and gynaecological and notes on capitalization and compounds.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list for words beginning with I, with preferred spellings, word-form choices and usage notes.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list for words beginning with L, with preferred spellings, distinctions between similar words and hyphenation notes.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list for words beginning with M and N, with preferred spellings, hyphenation and usage notes.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list for words beginning with O and the start of P, giving preferred spellings, hyphenation and capitalization choices.

Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list from words beginning with post- and pre- through to R, including terms such as Region and Regional Committee, with preferred spellings and capitalization notes.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list through R and into S, with preferred forms and distinctions between similar words such as sewage and sewerage.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list through S and into T, giving preferred spellings, hyphenation and capitalization choices.
Continues the alphabetical spelling and usage list from T through V, with preferred spellings, hyphenation and usage notes.
Finishes the alphabetical spelling and usage list with words beginning with W through Z, giving preferred spellings and distinctions between similar words such as waive and wave.
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Opens Annex 2, a table of Member States of the United Nations, specialized agency members and parties to the Court statute, giving short name, full name, adjective or people, and capital city, beginning with Afghanistan. It ends with a note that the United Nations keeps no official list of capitals.
Continues the Annex 2 table of country names, full names, adjectives and capital cities, covering entries from Benin to Côte d'Ivoire with footnotes on seats of government.
Continues the Annex 2 table of country names, full names, adjectives and capital cities, covering entries from Croatia to Georgia.
Continues the Annex 2 table of country names, full names, adjectives and capital cities, covering entries from Germany to Iran, with footnotes on preferred name forms.
Continues the Annex 2 table of country names, full names, adjectives and capital cities, covering entries from Kazakhstan to Mexico, with a note on the invariable form of Lao.
Continues the Annex 2 table of country names, full names, adjectives and capital cities, covering entries from Micronesia onward, with footnotes on name usage and seat of government.
Continues the Annex 2 table of country names, full names, adjectives and capital cities, covering entries from the Philippines to the Solomon Islands.
Continues the Annex 2 table of country names, full names, adjectives and capital cities, covering entries from Somalia to the United Arab Emirates.
Finishes the Annex 2 table of country names with the United Kingdom, United Republic of Tanzania, United States of America, Uruguay, Uzbekistan and Vanuatu, with notes on shorter permitted forms.
Near-empty page with no extractable text.

Opens Annex 3 on place names, with an alphabetical list of English or approved names beside their local or other names, starting at A. Asterisks mark WHO Member States and the text refers readers to Annex 2 for full names; extraction has jumbled the two columns.
Continues the Annex 3 alphabetical list of English or approved place names with local or other names, covering H to R. The two columns are interleaved by extraction.
Continues the Annex 3 alphabetical list of English or approved place names with local or other names, covering R to Z. The columns are jumbled by extraction.
Begins the second Annex 3 list, ordered by local or other name, with the corresponding English or approved name, covering names from A to roughly G.
Continues the Annex 3 list ordered by local or other name with the English or approved equivalent, covering entries from H to P.
Finishes the Annex 3 list ordered by local or other name with the English or approved equivalent, covering entries from R to Z.
Opens Annex 4, a two-column English and French glossary of terms used in manuscript mark-up and proof correction, covering typography and layout terms such as typeface, italic, roman and landscape.
Continues the English and French glossary of mark-up and proof-correction terms, including add, insert, delete, close up, transpose, stet and to be typeset.
